Temperature scaling is a post-hoc calibration technique that fits a single scalar parameter T on a held-out validation set to sharpen or soften a classifier's softmax outputs so that predicted probabilities match empirical frequencies. The central question here is: when the underlying label distribution shifts over time — because the model itself is being continuously updated and redeployed — does the temperature you fitted yesterday remain valid today? The key concepts in tension are (1) calibration (the statistical alignment between confidence and accuracy), (2) label shift (the marginal P(Y) changes while P(X|Y) stays fixed), and (3) the coupling problem — continuous model updating creates a feedback loop where each retraining changes the model's logit geometry, invalidating the scalar T that was fit to the previous version's logit scale.

What a beginner misses is that temperature scaling's validity rests on a stationarity assumption that is quietly violated the moment you start iterating the model. A beginner sees a well-calibrated model at deployment and assumes calibration is a solved problem; an expert knows that the logit norms tend to grow with continued fine-tuning (a known phenomenon in overconfident fine-tuned models), meaning T needs to increase monotonically just to stand still — and that's before accounting for the label-shift component changing the target frequencies the calibration is supposed to match. The real danger is that miscalibration becomes invisible in aggregate metrics while being severe in the tail classes that are shifting most rapidly, which is exactly where deployment decisions are highest-stakes.

Temperature scaling fits a single scalar to minimize expected calibration error (ECE) or negative log-likelihood (NLL) across all classes jointly — so T* is essentially a weighted compromise across per-class calibration needs, where the weights are the class marginals P(Y). If rare classes (which tend to have lower-confidence, softer logits in typical overparameterized models) become more frequent, the optimal T* decreases (sharpen the distribution) because those classes need higher confidence to be well-calibrated at their new prevalence. Conversely, if high-frequency, high-confidence majority classes dominate more heavily, T* increases to soften over-sharp predictions. Kull et al. Concretely, on ImageNet-scale models, Minderer et al. The expert worry is that monitoring aggregate ECE after label shift can show apparent stability (the majority-class calibration is fine) while minority-class calibration has catastrophically worsened — and because T* moved in the direction demanded by the majority, it actively made minority-class calibration worse.

Yes, there is a principled decomposition, and the distinction matters enormously for intervention. Logit-norm growth is a property of the model's weight geometry — specifically, the Frobenius norm of the final linear layer's weight matrix tends to increase during fine-tuning because gradient updates are not norm-constrained, and this manifests as a systematic increase in the scale of all logits, which temperature scaling can in principle correct by raising T*. Label-shift-induced miscalibration, by contrast, is a mismatch between the model's implicit prior (baked in during training via the empirical class frequencies) and the deployment distribution — this cannot be fixed by a scalar temperature because it requires reweighting the class-conditional outputs, not just rescaling them uniformly. Desai and Durrett (2020, "Calibration of Pre-trained Transformers") showed that for fine-tuned BERT-family models, the dominant source of miscalibration post-fine-tuning is logit-norm inflation rather than distributional shift, suggesting T* adjustment is the right first intervention there. But in continuously updated production systems — like those described in the context of Google's streaming recommendation models or Meta's DLRM-style architectures — where label distributions shift with user behavior, the label-shift component dominates over longer time horizons, and applying a higher T* without reweighting actually increases minority-class ECE as shown in the previous turn's reasoning. A clean diagnostic is to monitor the two signals separately: track the mean logit norm across batches (a proxy for weight-geometry drift) and track the KL divergence between training-time and deployment-time label marginals; if the former moves first and dominates, recalibrate T*; if the latter dominates, you need importance-weighted calibration (e.g., Platt scaling with reweighted validation data or prior-correction methods like those in Alexandari et al., 2020, "Maximum likelihood with bias-corrected calibration"). The practical consequence is that a single automated recalibration pipeline that only tunes T* will systematically underperform in label-shift-dominant regimes, giving false confidence that the system is well-calibrated when it has merely rebalanced its errors across classes.

In performative settings, the "true" P(Y) is not a fixed target but a functional of the model's deployment policy — Perdomo et al. (2020) formalize this as the performative stable distribution, P*(Y; θ), the distribution that the model induces at its own parameters θ, and calibration against this fixed point is the only coherent target because it is the only distribution the model will actually encounter at equilibrium. The problem is that this fixed point may not be unique, may be unstable, or may require the model to be miscalibrated in the classical sense to sustain it — for example, in a content recommendation system, a model that confidently predicts engagement will drive engagement, making its confident predictions self-fulfilling, which means the model appears well-calibrated not because its probabilities reflect an external reality but because it has shaped reality to match its probabilities. This collapses the standard frequentist grounding of calibration (that predicted probability p should match empirical frequency across exchangeable draws) because the draws are no longer exchangeable — each prediction changes the distribution of the next one. Brown and Calmon (2022, in the fairness literature on performative prediction) showed that in such systems, optimizing for classical ECE can lock the system into a high-confidence, self-reinforcing equilibrium that is well-calibrated on its own induced distribution but severely miscalibrated relative to any counterfactual distribution — meaning the calibration metric gives you no warning that you have drifted into a pathological regime. A more defensible redefinition of the calibration target is interventional calibration: the model's confidence in outcome Y should match the frequency of Y under a do-intervention that fixes the model's output and breaks the feedback loop, as formalized in causal calibration work by Zhao et al. (2021, "Right for Better Reasons") — but this requires either randomized experiments or strong causal assumptions about the feedback structure. Practically, this means that in performative systems, calibration evaluation cannot be done passively from logged data alone; you need held-out cohorts where the model's predictions are withheld or randomized, which most production ML systems are not instrumented to do, making the miscalibration silently undetectable.

The weakest sufficient assumption set for observational identification of the interventional calibration target is roughly: (1) existence of a valid instrument — a variable that affects the model's output but has no direct effect on the outcome except through the model's action, (2) monotonicity of the instrument's effect on the treatment (model-recommended action), and (3) exclusion restriction holding conditional on observed covariates. In fraud detection, a plausible instrument is the random assignment of cases to different analyst queues with heterogeneous review thresholds — the queue assignment affects whether the model's flag gets acted upon, but doesn't directly cause fraud, so you can use queue-induced variation to estimate what outcomes would have been absent the model's influence. The breakdown point for assumption (1) is subtle: in modern systems where the instrument itself was historically influenced by earlier model versions (e.g., queue thresholds were set based on past model confidence scores), the instrument is contaminated — it encodes the feedback loop rather than breaking it, a problem Angrist and Pischke flag generally but which is especially acute in ML-in-the-loop systems where "human decisions" are increasingly model-assisted. Assumption (3), the exclusion restriction, breaks in practice whenever the model's confidence score is visible to downstream decision-makers and influences their behavior independently of the recommended action — in clinical triage, if physicians see the model's 87% sepsis probability and order additional tests that change the outcome regardless of the triage decision, the instrument-to-outcome path is no longer exclusively through the treatment, and your IV estimate of interventional calibration is biased in an unquantifiable direction. A weaker alternative to full IV identification is sensitivity analysis under bounded confounding (Rosenbaum-style Γ bounds or the more recent Tan 2006 / Cinelli-Hazlett 2020 frameworks), which don't identify the interventional target exactly but bound how wrong your observational calibration estimate could be as a function of the unmeasured confounding strength — this is the practical state of the art in high-stakes settings, telling you not "here is the true calibration" but "if confounding is no stronger than Γ=2, the interventional ECE is within ±0.06 of what we observe." The deepest breakdown is systemic: all these identification strategies assume the causal graph is known and stable, but in a continuously updating model, the feedback structure itself changes with each retraining — the instrument valid under model version v_t may be invalid under v_{t+1} because the model has learned to exploit or correlate with the instrument, a form of Goodhart's Law applied to causal identification.

More directly, you can test the exclusion restriction's observable implication: if the instrument is valid, it should be independent of all observed covariates after conditioning on the treatment; a model that has learned to correlate with the instrument will cause the instrument to become predictable from the model's input features, which you can detect by regressing the instrument on the model's penultimate-layer embeddings and monitoring R² over model versions — an R² that rises from near-zero toward 0.1+ is a red flag that the instrument is being internalized. In a production pipeline, this translates to two concrete monitors: (1) a covariate balance dashboard that tracks standardized mean differences of input features across instrument strata (analogous to a randomization check in an RCT) recomputed after each model update, and (2) a cross-fit partial R² monitor that measures how much of the instrument's variance is explained by the model's features, with an alert threshold calibrated to the sensitivity bounds from your Rosenbaum analysis. The practical difficulty is that these tests have power only against detectable correlations in the observed feature space — a model can corrupt an instrument by learning a representation that correlates with the instrument's underlying generator without that correlation appearing in any hand-engineered feature, which is precisely the failure mode of deep models with high-dimensional embeddings. The architectural implication for a monitoring pipeline is that you need to store frozen snapshots of the model's penultimate embeddings at the time the instrument was validated, and re-run the exclusion test using those frozen embeddings against each new model version's predictions — if the new model's outputs are predictable from the old embeddings conditioned on the instrument, the instrument has been corrupted in a way the new model's feature space would obscure.
